title: Synapse GoPro Worker
description: Read-only Matrix federation endpoints served by the GoPro worker: traffic, upstream latency, and shadow-mode agreement with Synapse.

list.name: bucket
list.label: Bucket
list.description: Range window for rate() and histogram_quantile(). 'auto' scales with the dashboard time range (minimum 30s). Prometheus scrapes this worker every 15s and rate() needs two samples in the window, so 5s/10s/15s return nothing at all and 30s is the practical floor. At this server's federation volume even 1m often reads as zero between requests, which is why the default is 5m.

panels.title: Request rate
panels.description: Federation requests served per second across all three endpoints.

panels.title: Failure ratio
panels.description: Share of requests returning 5xx. 502 means the upstream Synapse worker was unreachable, so a sustained non-zero value here is an availability problem, not a Matrix one.

panels.title: p99 upstream latency
panels.description: 99th percentile time waiting on Synapse. This is the baseline the native implementation has to beat.

panels.title: Upstream errors
panels.description: Rate of requests that could not reach any Synapse worker.

panels.title: Client disconnects
panels.description: Requests where the remote server hung up before we answered. Routine for slow /state calls; a spike suggests we became too slow for remote timeouts.

panels.title: Worker restarts
panels.description: Process starts recorded against the diff log, preserved across deploys.

panels.title: Request rate by endpoint
panels.description: /state and /state_ids are the expensive ones; /event is usually the most frequent.

panels.title: Upstream latency percentiles
panels.description: Time spent waiting on the Synapse worker, by endpoint. NOTE: this covers every request, including cancelled ones. To compare against the native implementation use the 'Native vs Synapse latency' panel, which measures both over the same requests.

panels.title: Status codes
panels.description: 403 is normal federation traffic (server not in room, or barred by a server ACL). 404 on /event is normal too. Watch for 502 and 'none'.

panels.title: Serving mode
panels.description: How each request was answered. During cutover this shows traffic shifting from proxy to native; a native fallback appears as proxy traffic on a native endpoint.

panels.title: Upstream latency distribution
panels.description: Full latency spread. Large rooms show up as a slow tail on /state.

panels.title: Response size percentiles
panels.description: /state on a large room returns megabytes of PDUs; this is what makes it costly.

panels.title: Upstream requests skipped
panels.description: Requests never forwarded because the client had already hung up -- work Synapse is spared, roughly 2.55s of its database time each on /state_ids. Deliberately separate from the cancelled-request count: a request cancelled after we forwarded is not work avoided.

panels.title: Clients that went away
panels.description: Remote servers hanging up. Routine for federation traffic and not a fault here -- Tuwunel-style servers hang up on /state_ids constantly -- but a sharp rise means something changed in how long we take to answer.

panels.title: Overall match rate
panels.description: Agreement with Synapse across the whole run, restored from stats.json on restart. Empty until an endpoint is put into shadow mode.

panels.title: Comparisons
panels.description: Total shadow comparisons performed, cumulative across restarts.

panels.title: Mismatches
panels.description: Total disagreements. Must be zero, and stay zero for the soak window, before an endpoint is promoted.

panels.title: Time since last mismatch
panels.description: The promotion clock. It restarts every time the two implementations disagree. Green at 7 days.

panels.title: Dropped diff records
panels.description: Records lost because the writer queue was full. Any non-zero value means the diff log is incomplete and the promotion gate cannot be trusted.

panels.title: Diff log write errors
panels.description: Failures writing the log or its stats. Usually a full or read-only disk.

panels.title: Match rate by endpoint
panels.description: Endpoints are promoted individually, so each is tracked separately.

panels.title: Mismatch rate
panels.description: New disagreements per second. A flat zero line is what earns promotion.

panels.title: Native vs Synapse latency (same requests)
panels.description: The comparison the project exists to make. Both series cover ONLY the requests shadow comparison measured. Do not compare shadow_duration against gopro_upstream_duration_seconds: that one includes cancelled requests, which are skipped here and are by definition the slow ones, so it flatters the native implementation.

panels.title: Auth verdicts
panels.description: we_accept_synapse_rejects is the promotion blocker: we accepted a request Synapse rejected on the merits. synapse_key_fetch_failed is different -- Synapse could not obtain the origin's key, so it never judged the signature, and its 401 says nothing about whether accepting was right.

panels.title: Comparisons skipped
panels.description: Requests not counted either way, so the match rate covers less traffic than it appears. upstream_key_fetch_failed and upstream_rate_limited both mean Synapse never produced an answer to compare against -- the second is Synapse shedding load, which our limiter deliberately does not mirror while proxying or shadowing. A sustained rise in upstream_rate_limited means Synapse is struggling with traffic we are absorbing.

panels.title: Comparison outcomes by kind
panels.description: What comparisons concluded, not just match-versus-not. body_mismatch is a content disagreement; status_mismatch means the sides returned different HTTP statuses; native_error and native_timeout mean we could not produce an answer at all, which on the request path would have been a fallback. The series existed long before this panel: the dashboard could show that a mismatch happened but not what kind it was.

panels.title: Digest blind spots
panels.description:
PDUs served on /state carrying prev_content or prev_sender. Not defects: both fields are in Synapse's unsigned allowlist, remote servers send them and Synapse stores them verbatim -- 9,300 events across 158 rooms here. Both sides serve them identically.

What this counts is how often the digest compares blind. Canonical drops these fields from both sides, because a digest cannot apply a tolerance asymmetrically the way Equal does, so for every PDU counted here a disagreement about those two fields would not have been caught. Read a clean /state match rate against this number rather than on its own.

panels.title: Expired remote keys
panels.description: Origins that presented a valid-looking but expired key. mautrix verifies the self-signature without checking valid_until_ts on a freshly fetched response, so this check is ours. Non-zero means remote servers with broken key servers, not a fault here.

panels.title: Soaking since
panels.description: How long the accumulated comparison evidence covers. The cumulative mismatch ratio never clears by design, so it is only meaningful against this: a ratio computed over a soak that began before a fix landed says nothing about the code running now. Read it alongside 'Time since last mismatch', which is the number that actually matters.

panels.title: Served natively
panels.description: Answers produced by us and sent to a remote server. In shadow mode this is zero: nothing we compute is served.

panels.title: Verified share
panels.description: Fraction of served answers that were afterwards checked against Synapse. This is the number a promotion decision rests on: a canary that serves but does not verify is worse than shadow mode, because the answers nobody checked are the ones that left the building.

panels.title: Fell back to Synapse
panels.description: Requests sampled for the canary that were proxied instead. A canary where everything falls back is shadow mode wearing a different label.

panels.title: Fallback reasons
panels.description: Why a sampled request was not answered by us. client_gone means the remote server hung up before we could answer -- common here, since Tuwunel-style servers do it constantly, and not a defect. timeout means our own budget expired, which is worth investigating. auth_rejected means we could not verify the signature. error and panic point at our code.

panels.title: Native answer latency
panels.description: Time to produce an answer that was actually served, over the whole selected range rather than per bucket: a canary serves few requests, and any bucket with no observations yields NaN and draws as an empty panel. Unlike the shadow histogram this describes what remote servers experienced.

panels.title: Fallback outcome at Synapse
panels.description: What happened at Synapse for requests we gave up on -- the question these metrics were added to answer. Without it a fallback was invisible past the moment it happened, because the upstream histogram covers every request and cannot isolate the abandoned one. upstream=canceled means the remote server had already gone, which on this deployment is the common case rather than the rare one.

panels.title: What a fallback cost the client
panels.description: End-to-end time for a request that fell back: our attempt plus Synapse's, in series. This is why the serving budget is 5s rather than the shadow timeout's 30s -- the whole budget is spent before Synapse is even asked.

panels.title: Verification waiting for a slot
panels.description:
Verifications of a served answer that found every comparison slot busy and waited. Shadow comparison drops instantly when busy; verification waits, because it is the only check on something a remote server actually received.

This is the early warning. While it climbs the verified share is still 1.0 -- the waits are succeeding. It only falls once a wait times out, which shows up as skipped{reason=busy}. Read the two together: this rising means the worker is coping, not comfortable, and is the signal to add upstream capacity before evidence starts being lost.

panels.title: Native p50
panels.description: What a remote server waited for a median natively served request: verification plus the answer. Quantiles are taken over the whole selected range rather than per bucket: at this volume a bucket with no observations yields NaN and the panel draws empty. These series do not exist until the first answer is served natively -- Prometheus creates counter and histogram children on first increment -- so this row is empty in proxy and shadow mode, and after every restart until the first native answer.

panels.title: Native p90
panels.description: End-to-end, 90th percentile. Quantiles are taken over the whole selected range rather than per bucket: at this volume a bucket with no observations yields NaN and the panel draws empty.

panels.title: Native p99
panels.description: End-to-end, 99th percentile. This is the number to compare against Synapse's tail, which is where the advantage has always been -- not at p50.

panels.title: Answer p99
panels.description: The answer alone, excluding verification: state resolution, cache lookups and serialisation. This is the part we control and optimise. If it is flat while Native p99 rises, the cost is verification, not our code.

panels.title: Verification overhead
panels.description: Native p50 minus Answer p50, i.e. what X-Matrix verification costs a median request. Normally microseconds against a warm key cache; an origin whose keys must be fetched over the network costs a round trip, and against an unhealthy key server that has meant tens of seconds. Read it as an indication, not an exact figure: a difference of quantiles is not the quantile of differences.

targets.expr: (histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le) (rate(gopro_native_request_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$endpoint", job=~"$job"}[$__range])))) - (histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le) (rate(gopro_native_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$endpoint", job=~"$job"}[$__range]))))

panels.title: Served natively
panels.description: Rate of answers produced and sent by us. Judge a canary by this, never by assuming the configured percentage: sampling hashes the event ID, so concentrated traffic on a few hot events can push the served share well below or above N.

panels.title: Native latency percentiles by endpoint
panels.description: End-to-end time for requests we served, per endpoint. Log scale, because p50 and p99 differ by orders of magnitude. Unlike the shadow histogram this covers only answers that actually reached a remote server. Uses $bucket rather than the full range so change over time is visible; if it draws empty, widen $bucket -- see the stats above, which do not have that problem. These series do not exist until the first answer is served natively -- Prometheus creates counter and histogram children on first increment -- so this row is empty in proxy and shadow mode, and after every restart until the first native answer.

panels.title: Where the time goes: verification vs answer
panels.description: The gap between the two pairs is X-Matrix verification. gopro_native_duration_seconds times only the answer, which is the part we optimise but not the part a remote server waits for -- verification sits in front of it and needs a network key fetch for any origin whose keys are not cached. The rate limiter is outside both: it is acquired before the attempt begins and is measured separately by gopro_rate_limit_queue_wait_seconds, so this gap is verification and nothing else.

panels.title: Native latency distribution
panels.description: Full spread of what remote servers waited for. A bimodal picture means cache hits and misses are resolving very differently -- expected on /state_ids, where a cold large room is orders of magnitude slower than a warm one.

panels.title: Native answers served
panels.description: Throughput of what we answered, by endpoint and status. 403 and 404 are ordinary federation outcomes here -- a host not in the room, or an event we do not have -- not errors. Falling back to Synapse is counted separately in the Canary row and does not appear as a status.

panels.title: Rejected (429)
panels.description: Requests refused outright. If this is non-zero while Synapse is not answering 429, our rc_federation is tighter than Synapse's and we are shedding load it would serve. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Delayed
panels.description: Requests deliberately slowed rather than refused. Throttling starts here, well before any rejection, so this is the earlier warning of the two. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Origins rejected
panels.description: Distinct servers rejected since startup. Answers whether throttling is one noisy server or many, which the counters alone cannot say. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Servers tracked
panels.description: Origin servers with live limiter state. Also a rough count of who is talking to us. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: p99 limiter wait
panels.description: Latency the limiter itself adds. This is time we impose, not time we measure, so it is excluded from the native-vs-Synapse comparison. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Rejection share
panels.description: Share of requests refused by the limiter. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Rate limiting by endpoint
panels.description: Rejections and delays per endpoint. There is deliberately no per-origin series: this server has exchanged keys with tens of thousands of others, and a label per origin would be a cardinality explosion. Which server is being limited is in the worker logs, at warn for rejections and info for delays. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Limiter wait time
panels.description: How long requests spend waiting on the limiter, by percentile. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: State group hit rate
panels.description: The one that matters. Resolving state at an event is by far the most expensive read; a state group's contents never change, so a hit turns a full recursive walk into a map lookup. Measured cold-vs-warm on the largest room here: 1.04s against 2us.

panels.title: Event hit rate
panels.description: Stored event JSON, which does not change.

panels.title: Cache memory
panels.description: Total across all caches. Compare against the configured bounds.

panels.title: Evictions
panels.description: Entries dropped to stay within the size bound. Sustained evictions on state_groups mean the bound is too small for the working set, and the expensive resolutions are being recomputed.

panels.title: Entries cached
panels.description: Total entries across all caches.

panels.title: Hit rate by cache
panels.description: Fraction of lookups served from memory, since startup. Caches are empty after a restart, so expect this to climb rather than start high.

panels.title: Cache size against bound
panels.description: Bytes held versus the configured limit. A cache pinned at its bound with steady evictions is undersized.

panels.title: Lookups per second
panels.description: Hits and misses by cache.

panels.title: Native latency against cache hit rate
panels.description: The point of the cache. Native p99 should fall as the state group hit rate rises.

panels.title: Filtered state from cache
panels.description: Share of /event's filtered state-group lookups answered from cache rather than a recursive walk of state_groups_state. 'filtered_cache' is the per-(group,filter) cache; 'state_cache' means the whole map happened to be resident.

panels.title: Filtered state lookups
panels.description: Filtered state-group resolutions by query kind and source. 'database' means a recursive CTE over state_groups_state; 'cache' means the whole map was already resolved.

panels.title: Invalidation stream
panels.description: The caches serve only while this is Connected. While it is Disconnected they are empty and every request goes to Postgres — a latency cost, never a correctness one.

panels.title: Cache flushes
panels.description: Times the caches were emptied in the window: a purge, a (re)connect, or a row we could not parse. Occasional flushes are normal; a steady stream means the subscription is flapping.

panels.title: Malformed rows
panels.description: Replication rows we failed to parse. Each one empties the caches, because an unparsed row may have been the purge that makes us wrong. Anything above zero means Synapse's format has moved.

panels.title: Replication commands
panels.description: Everything arriving on the channel. RDATA/caches is the one that can affect us; presence and receipts dominate by volume and are ignored.

panels.title: Cache invalidations
panels.description: Invalidation rows by Synapse cache function. ph_cache_fake and dr_cache_fake mean events were deleted and empty every cache; 'ignored' is everything we do not mirror.

panels.title: Invalidation stream age
panels.description: Time since the last replication message. The caches are armed only while this subscription is healthy, so a stream that has gone quiet is the difference between a cache that is safe and one that is silently stale. Quiet periods are normal overnight; hours of silence during European daytime are not.

panels.title: Diff log throughput
panels.description: Records written and files rotated. A soak whose evidence is being dropped or failing to write is not a soak, and rotations tell you how fast the retained history is being consumed.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: One process replacing N Python workers: goroutine count should track in-flight requests, not grow without bound.

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: Resident memory. The point of consolidating workers is a lower total than the Python fleet it replaces.

panels.title: GC pause
panels.description: Stop-the-world pause time. A large shared state cache shows up here first.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: Cores in use. One whole core reads as 1.0. This process is idle almost all the time, which is itself informative: the endpoints are reactive, not ambient.

panels.title: Resident memory
panels.description: RSS, including the caches. Compare against a Synapse worker: each of those holds its own private cache, so N workers duplicate what one process here holds once.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: A rising floor means goroutines are leaking; shadow and canary work is bounded by a semaphore and should return to a low baseline.

panels.title: Open files
panels.description: Sockets and files. Climbing without bound means connections are not being released.

panels.title: GC pauses
panels.description: Collections per second. The caches are byte-bounded, so this should stay flat rather than tracking traffic.

panels.title: Heap in use
panels.description: Live heap. The gap between this and RSS is memory returned to the OS lazily.

panels.title: CPU: this worker vs Synapse's federation reader
panels.description: The scalability argument in one panel. A Synapse worker is effectively single-core, which is why N of them are run; this process uses all cores. Note the comparison is not like-for-like -- av-requests also serves the client API -- so read it as an order of magnitude, not a ratio.

panels.title: Memory: this worker vs Synapse's federation reader
panels.description: Each Synapse worker holds a private cache, so a fleet duplicates it N times; this process holds one shared cache. Same caveat: av-requests also serves the client API.
